svg.title: Robin Hood hashing against linear probing: the tables slot by slot, probes per lookup against load, and the ratios
svg.text: the same average walk to a key, a far shorter worst one
Every picture and number is computed by harness.py or read from its log.
How a hash table with open addressing finds a key, and the words used below; the number on a card is the panel that shows it.
A key has a home slot
The table is a row of slots. A hash of the
key names one of them, its home slot:
If that slot is taken, the key goes into the
next free one: linear probing. How far
from home it ends up is its
A lookup walks the same way. Every slot
it looks at is a probe. A key that is there
is a hit; one that is not, a miss, shows
Robin Hood changes one thing: when
two keys want a slot, the one further from
home gets it and the other moves on.

svg.text: Two tables, the same keys, slot by slot
colour: how far a key sits from its home slot
the furthest key is 622 slots from home
slots 10 to 33: how far each key sits from home
the furthest key is 36 slots from home
slots 10 to 33: how far each key sits from home

Two tables of 4,096 slots, one cell per slot, row after row, with the same 3,686 keys put in in the same order (load 0.90). Which slots are taken does not depend on the rule, only who sits where: the two pictures have the same

empty slots, and the distances from home add up to the same 22,789 in both, 6.18 per key (checked while drawing). What differs is how that total is shared out. linear probing leaves the keys that came last far out, up to 622
slots; Robin Hood keeps every key within 36.
What a lookup costs as the table fills
load α: the share of slots in use
Counted in a table of 32,768 slots that is filled step by step; the misses with 4,096
keys that are not in it. One probe means the key was at home.
The pale bands are Knuth's formulas for linear probing: ½(1 + 1/(1−α)) for a hit
and ½(1 + 1/(1−α)2) for a miss. At α = 0.90 they give 5.50 and 50.5; the counts
Robin Hood leaves the average hit where it was: the two rules give the same
number at every load (checked), so one curve stands for both. It shortens the
worst hit, 46 probes instead of 1,575 at α = 0.95, and a miss can stop at the first
key that sits closer to home than the walk is long.
above 1×, Robin Hood is the cheaper one
lookup, the key is not there
the same probes; 0.4 keys moved on per insert
lookup, the key is not there
the same probes; 18.1 keys moved on per insert
time per operation: measured on one machine
How many times cheaper Robin Hood is than linear probing: at load 0.90 a miss
The clock agrees in direction, not in size: that miss is 4.0 times faster, and a hit,
although it looks at the same slots, takes 1.9 times as long. This table is plain
Python, where the one extra comparison per probe costs as much as the probe.
Times are medians of five runs on one machine, kept in logs/bench.txt; the
counts are exact and are recomputed whenever the figure is built.
